Excellencies, delegates, distinguished guests, we're pleased to welcome you to this ARIA Formula meeting. entitled Safe Education to Prevent the Recruitment and Use of Children in Armed Conflict. We'd like to thank Greece, Liberia, Austria, Japan, and Uruguay for their co-sponsorship of this event and for their commitment to this agenda. Panama and the co-sponsors have convened an ARIA Formula United Nations Security Council meeting on the Red Hand Day to specifically highlight that education is a right and that a safe, inclusive, and continuous education is a strategic tool to prevent the recruitment and the use of children in armed conflict. It's also a tool that serves as a pillar to reintegrate those affected by armed conflict. Excellencies, it's an honor for us to have our distinguished briefers with us today, and I will now proceed to give them the floor. Firstly, we are pleased to give the floor to Ms. Vanessa Fraser, Special Representative of the Secretary-General for Children and Armed Conflict, with whom we were able to share our experience during her involvement on the Security Council when Panama was recently an observer on the Security Council in 2024. Vanessa, you have the floor.

Thank you, Thank you, Ambassador. Excellencies, ladies and gentlemen, I thank the Permanent Mission of Panama and the co-sponsors Austria, Greece, Japan, Liberia for convening this important meeting at such a critical time. It is an honor to take part in this discussion to highlight a truth that children living through conflict remind us of every day: education is not a luxury. It is a lifeline. It protects, heals, inspires, and offers the promise of a different future. From country to country, the testimonies collected by my office are remarkably consistent. Children themselves say education is their number one priority when rebuilding their lives after grave violations. It offers structure, restores dignity, and reconnects them them with their communities. Yet, too many children are denied this fundamental right. Today, more than 250 million children are out of school globally, many because of conflict and insecurity. When education collapses, so do the protective systems that keep children safe— safe from recruitment, abduction, sexual violence, including forced marriage and other grave violations. When war breaks out, children lose far more than their classrooms. Schools are destroyed or occupied, teachers are displaced or attacked, and the simple act of walking to school becomes dangerous. In 2024 alone, 1,265 attacks on schools and related personnel were verified by the United Nations in 26 conflict situations. In 2025, based on preliminary data, such attacks were verified at a similarly high level. Schools were bombed, looted, and burned. Teachers were abducted or killed for trying to educate their students. Children were attacked on their way to school or in— or while in class. Notably, government forces were the main perpetrators of attacks schools and hospitals in 2024. Also of concern is the presence of explosive remnants of war near schools and in other places frequented by children, often with deadly consequences, which underline that mine action must urgently be prioritized to protect the most vulnerable. In countries such as Afghanistan, Burkina Faso, Mali, Nigeria, Somalia, and Syria, hundreds of schools have been forced to close due to insecurity, depriving children of education and exposing them to further violence. In Afghanistan, girls remain particularly and systematically affected, including due to the suspension of girls' education by the Taliban. Across several contexts, armed groups have also attempted to control curricula or use schools as sites for indoctrination, further undermining the right to quality education. These attacks must stop. The military use of schools must end. Every child, everywhere, has the right to an education free from violence. I call on all Member States and all parties to conflict to take urgent measures to protect schools, students and teachers, including by endorsing the Safe School Schools Declaration and developing national action plans for its implementation. Education is not only a fundamental right, it is a cornerstone of peace, stability, and development. Excellencies, education is central to both preventing child recruitment and youth and ensuring sustainable reintegration of children formerly associated with armed forces and groups. As stated in the 2007 Paris Principles, education is an essential component of reintegration programs. Returning to school is often the first step towards rebuilding a child's confidence and future prospects. It provides skills, restores normalcy, and helps communities accept and welcome children back. Education also contributes directly to sustainable peace. We must invest not only in ceasefires, but also in classrooms, in teachers, curricula, and inclusive systems that reach girls, displaced children, and those who have been most marginalized. Yet the scale of today's challenges is sobering. The Secretary-General's most recent report on children and armed conflict verified more than 41,000 grave violations against children in 2024 alone. These figures illustrate not just the magnitude of suffering, but also the obstacles standing between children and their right to education. Security Council Resolution 2601 recognizes the essential link between peace, security, and education. I welcome steps taken by several Member States to strengthen national protection frameworks, including countries that have criminalized attacks on schools and/or have domesticated the Safe Schools Declaration into national policy. But we must also strengthen implementation. Within the 2030 Agenda, the Education 2030 Framework for Action urges us to address education in emergencies and protracted crises. Supporting Member States in building inclusive, resilient and responsive educational systems is essential. Teachers are at the heart of these systems. In conflict and post-conflict settings, they are not only educators; they are frontline responders, protectors and sources of psychosocial support. Competent and empowered teachers are indispensable to reintegration efforts and to the long-term resilience of affected communities. My Office will continue to work with parties to conflict to prevent and end attacks on schools and education personnel through joint protection and prevention plans. I will continue advocating for an end to the military use of schools. We will also strengthen cooperation with partners such as UNICEF and UNESCO present today, including through initiatives that expand across to connectivity for students— that expand access, sorry, to connectivity for students and protect and support teachers working in conflict zones. As such, my Office recently developed with UNESCO the Guidance Toolkit for Teachers and Educators on Education for Children and Young People Formerly Associated with Armed Forces and Armed Groups. We launched it this month in New York. This is not merely a set of guidelines, it is a vital resource offering hope and healing to children whose lives have been shattered by war. I call on governments to prioritize education in their recovery efforts, and we, as an international community, must amplify the voices of children affected by armed conflict, ensuring they are heard, protected, and empowered. We must also support communities that remain crucial partners in embracing education and reintegration efforts with their sights set on the future. Every child affected by conflict deserves more than survival. They deserve a future. Protecting education is one of the most meaningful ways to offer them that future. By safeguarding schools today, we help build the foundations of sustainable peace tomorrow. I would like to close with the words of a child who participated in our #ProveItMatters campaign. He wrote, a school is the only place a child can walk in as the person they are and walk out as what they dream to be. Dear leaders, protect our schools today and we will protect the world tomorrow.

Thank you.

I thank Ms. Fraser for that briefing. I'm now pleased to be able to give the floor to Ms. Catherine Russell, Executive Director of UNICEF.

Thank you very much, Ambassador Alfaro de Alba, for convening today's ARIA Forum meeting, and to Greece, Austria, Japan, and Uruguay for co-hosting this really important discussion. It's a privilege to join you to reflect on the essential role education plays in preventing the recruitment and use of children in armed conflict. Excellencies, today, hundreds of millions of children, nearly 1 in 5 globally, live in countries where there is a war or other violent conflict. Every year, tens of thousands of children are killed or injured in armed conflict, and that number is only increasing. In addition, many of these children are malnourished and unable to go to school. As a result, children's education is increasingly under direct attack. Since the Security Council adopted Resolution 1612 in 2005, the United Nations has verified more than 14,000 attacks on schools and over 3,000 instances of military use of schools— nearly 2 attacks a day for 2 decades. The rate of these attacks is rising, and more than half have occurred in just the past 10 years. The Gaza Strip alone has seen 97% of its schools damaged or destroyed since 2023. In countries such as the DRC, Myanmar, and Ukraine, hundreds of schools have been looted, burned, and attacked with explosive weapons such as shelling and airstrikes. These attacks are grave violations against children, frontal assaults on children's safety, dignity, and future. When schools are attacked or occupied, children lose far more than learning opportunities. They lose protective spaces, opportunities to develop socially with their peers, and access to essential services such as school feeding, healthcare, and mental health support. They may also miss out on life-saving information about the risks posed by explosive remnants of war. Children who are out of school face significantly heightened risks of exploitation, child labor, child marriage, trafficking, and recruitment into armed groups. Protecting education means keeping schools safe and ensuring that parties to conflict refrain from using them for military purposes. Excellencies, we all know that education is both life-saving and life-changing. It is a powerful tool to prevent recruitment. When children can access safe, inclusive, and quality learning environments, they gain structure, nutritious meals, psychosocial support, essential services, and a sense of normalcy. UNICEF's experience shows that an integrated approach to education, protection, and peacebuilding is especially effective in preventing the recruitment of children. This includes safe learning spaces, accelerated learning for children who have missed school, and equipping teachers to support children at risk. It also means combining education with mental health support and community engagement and pathways to further learning or skills. UNICEF promotes the protection of schools from attack and military use by advocating with parties to comply with international law and advocating for member states to endorse and implement the Safe Schools Declaration Act. We work to expand access to formal and non-formal learning for conflict-affected children. This includes children who are displaced or living as refugees. At the community level, UNICEF works with parents, youth networks, and local leaders to strengthen protective environments and identify children at risk. We support education-based reintegration for children formerly associated with armed groups, and we help strengthen education systems and teacher capacity to create safe, inclusive learning environments and refer children to appropriate services. Excellency, safe education can effectively prevent child recruitment and the use of children by armed groups. but this requires collective action. UNICEF is urging all member states to endorse and to implement the Safe Schools Declaration and to adopt policies that protect schools, students, and teachers while ensuring accountability for grave rights violations. Education should be systematically integrated into international action plans on children in armed conflict. Member states should also provide sustained and flexible financing to guarantee safe, inclusive, and quality education in conflict-affected affected settings. UNICEF continues to call on parties to end attacks on education, the military use of schools, and the recruitment and use of children. Those listed in the annexes of the Secretary-General's Report on Children in Armed Conflict should promptly engage with the United Nations to develop and implement action plans that protect children and prevent further violations. Excellencies, at UNICEF, we believe that education protects children today while helping build the foundations for peace tomorrow. With that in mind, I'd like to close with an urgent request to this Council. I urge you to unequivocally denounce grave violations against children, to reaffirm that such actions are never acceptable and must never be normalized, to consistently call for accountability, and to use the influence you hold with parties to armed conflict to help protect children. Safe education is more than a development investment. It's a vital protection measure and a cornerstone of sustainable peace. By ensuring that children can learn in safety and dignity, we can finally help break cycles of violence. Thank you very much.
I'd now like to give the floor to Mr. Elliot Mickenberg, Director of the UNESCO Liaison Office in New York.

You have the floor. Thank you, Mr. President, Excellencies, dear colleagues. Let me start by thanking the Permanent Mission of Panama and the co-sponsors for convening this important discussion today. I also wish to express appreciation to the SRSG for Children in Armed Conflict and the Executive Director of UNICEF, valued partners of UNESCO in advancing the right to education for all. In an interview here in New York City, Ismail Behah, a former child soldier from Sierra Leone, said, and I quote, if I hadn't gone to school, I wouldn't be here today, end quote. His words capture what education makes possible for a child rebuilding his life after demobilization. Our experience shows that education, when it functions, is one of the most powerful tools we have to prevent recruitment, protect children, and support their reintegration. I will focus my intervention on each of these 3 pillars. On prevention, children become associated with armed groups for many reasons. Some are abducted, others join to escape poverty. For these children, education is often the strongest alternative pathway. Expanding access to formal, non-formal, and informal education, especially technical and vocational training linked to real labor market needs, offers meaningful choices to children and young people. When they experience the dignity of learning and earning, and when hope and prospect for the future is restored, the pool of armed conflicts— of armed groups, sorry, weakens. They choose learning over violence. This reality is stark in Cox's Bazar in Bangladesh, the world's largest refugee settlement. Recent funding cuts have forced the closure of vocational programs once serving over 8,000 young people. These are not just program losses, they are protection failures. Adolescents leave the camp searching for opportunity, increasing their exposure to risk. Education is not only a right; in crisis settings, it is a shield. On protection: for the children and young people who are in schools, ensuring the continuity of education during conflict is essential to protect them from recruitment. As violence escalates, it is critical that schools remain safe, stable spaces that foster cohesion. In Haiti, with the EU's support, UNESCO has launched a program in the northeast to reinforce community schools serving tens of thousands of students. And within this context, as was mentioned by previous speakers, teachers play an essential role. They are often the first adults to recognize signs of trauma, vulnerability, or recruitment risks, making them a critical line of protection for children. With adequate training and support, teachers become stabilizing figures, anchors of trust and belonging. Yet teaching in crisis requires far more than— is not just about delivering lessons. It demands navigating trauma, insecurity, supporting students with widely different experiences, and creating spaces where healing and learning can happen together. And teachers themselves face insecurity, displacement, and the emotional weight of supporting traumatized learners. To support teachers on the front line, UNESCO and the Office of the SRSG for Children in Armed Conflict have developed a global guidance toolkit with concrete, context-sensitive strategies for creating safe, inclusive, trauma-informed learning. This guidance is now being adapted across emergency contexts worldwide. And we call on all Member States to ensure that these guidelines are effectively deployed where it is most needed, through endorsement in national education systems, support for training and dissemination, and integration in emergency and post-conflict recovery frameworks. Last but not least, when higher education students and young professionals are forcibly displaced, it is important to ensure that their education counts, that their credentials are valid, and that their prior learning is acknowledged, so the pull towards recruitment weakens. Recognition is not a bureaucratic formality, it is a protection mechanism. 2 UNESCO instruments provide exactly this foundation: the Global Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications and the UNESCO Qualifications Passport. Ensuring displaced learners can re-enter education or employment quickly, even when documents of prior learning are missing. On reintegration: Reintegrating former child soldiers into civilian life is a profound process of healing and rebuilding. Many children have been forced to commit violent acts or have endured deep psychological harms. Mental health and psychological support must be at the centre of reintegration. And education is essential to this process. Classrooms must be spaces where peace and reconciliation are taught and lived. We must ask whether learning equips children with civic values, empathy, and the ability to engage across differences. They are not soft skills. They are the foundations of social cohesion and the strongest defense against hate-based narratives exploited by armed groups. The quality and relevance of education— what children learn, how they learn, and the values embedded in learning environments— is of utmost importance. In Sierra Leone, for example, we supported the development of the National Civic Education Strategy, the Cotton Tree Strategy, launched in 2024, which reinforces reconciliation and cohesion through education, youth engagement, and public awareness. To conclude, Excellencies, safe, inclusive, and continuous quality education is one of the most efficient preventative, protective, and reintegrative systems for children and youth. As violations rise, we must strengthen these pillars together. The Security Council has provided a solid foundation, especially through Resolutions 1998 and 2601, which protect schools, students, and teachers from attack. UNESCO stands ready to support Member States and work closely with the Office of the SRSG for Children in Armed Conflict and UNICEF to ensure that every child in conflict-affected regions has access to education that protects, empowers and restores hope. Because, as Ismail Beya reminds us, education can be the bridge between a child's past and a future once thought impossible. I thank you for your attention.

I'd like to thank Mr. Minkenberg for that statement, and I'm pleased now to be able to give the floor to Mr. Johnny César Étienne, Save the Children Haiti's Operations Director. You have the floor, sir.

Now we are watching it happen again. and include dedicated child protection advisors. These safeguards must be swiftly and transparently implemented. Second, we need to cut off the stream of recruitment where we can. Fund local, integrated, child-focused programs that address the interconnected crises driving children toward armed groups. It shields children from violence Exploitation, sexual abuse, and remains our most powerful counter-recruitment tool. If Haiti is to have a road to recovery, it must begin in the classroom. I thank Mr. Étienne for that briefing. Excellencies, We have a long list of speakers today and we're particularly pleased to see that. We want to make sure that everybody is able to take the floor. Therefore, we would encourage delegations to please respect the speaking time limit which is of 3 minutes. I'm now pleased to be able to give the floor to members of the Security Council. If you'll allow, I would like to begin with an opening statement in my capacity as National Representative. Excellencies, distinguished guests, allow me to begin with a simple but perhaps powerful image. In many places around the world today, a child walks to school carrying a notebook under their arm. But in other places, they walk carrying a weapon. The difference here isn't down to their talent, their will, or their worth. It depends to a large extent on whether or not they have had access to a safe school. Because when childhood is trapped between fear, hunger, and an absent state, education stops being a tangible right. And survival becomes a priority. And it is there, in that vacuum, that recruitment finds fertile ground. That's why Panama, together with Austria, Greece, Japan, Liberia, and Uruguay, have convened this ARIA Formula meeting. specifically on Red Hand Day, as a reminder that child recruitment doesn't start with a bullet. Rather, it starts when we fail to protect safe environments, real opportunities, and effective protection systems. The data sound this out. According to the United Nations, in 2024, there were more than 41,000 verified violations, serious violations against children in armed conflict, including 7,402 verified cases of recruitment and a 44% rise of attacks on schools. This isn't a distant reality. Indeed, in Latin America and the Caribbean, UNICEF has warned that there is persistent recruitment of children by armed groups and criminal networks fueled by illicit economies, including all forms of weapons trafficking, a lack of state presence, territorial control by gangs, and prolonged disruptions to schooling that all enhance children's vulnerability to coercion, displacement, and widespread violence. So the inevitable question is, what else can we do, each of us within our own realms of responsibility? Firstly, we can protect education as essential civil infrastructure— civilian infrastructure. And we can unambiguously condemn attacks on schools and the military use of schools. Initiatives such as the Safe Schools Declaration that has already been supported by 123 states provides a practical roadmap to curb risks and to protect both students and teachers. At the same time, investing in preventive measures in areas with a higher likelihood of recruitment is important. These include communities with extreme poverty, displacement, school closures, and chronic violence. This also includes providing psychosocial support, reintegration, and real opportunities for adolescents. Finally, it means demanding accountability. Impunity fuels and protects perpetrators. Victim-centred justice sends out another important message: that victims are not alone. The international community is not looking the other way. Panama is talking from its own history and its own experience. We chose to be a country without an army, with restrictions on the right to bear arms, and we firmly believe that no child should bear arms either. We want to use this voice to build bridges, to galvanize wills, and to support an inalienable objective, which is that every child should be able to choose to carry a notebook rather than a gun. Thank you. It's my pleasure now to be able to give the floor to members of the Security Council. The delegation of Greece, you have the floor.

Thank you, Chair. Greece supports Panama's initiative to convene this meeting on safe education as a strategic tool to prevent the recruitment and use of children in armed conflict and to support their reintegration. I would also like to thank the briefers for their valuable insights and reaffirm Greece's full support for the mandate of the Special Representative of the Secretary-General for children in armed conflict, as well as for the indispensable work of UNICEF and UNESCO. 24 years after its designation, the International Day Against the Use of Child Soldiers remains relevant, reminding us of a painful truth. As we speak, thousands of children are recruited and used in armed conflicts. Reintegration is not only essential for the children themselves. It is also a core component of conflict prevention, peacebuilding, inclusive societies, social cohesion and development. In this context, safe education is not only a right; it is a strategic investment in peace and security. Yet, in situations of armed conflict, children are deprived of this right. When educational facilities are attacked, used for military purposes or destroyed, children lose not only access to learning but also a protective framework that offers stability and psychosocial support. Out-of-school children are exposed to many risks, including recruitment, abduction, sexual and gender-based violence. Prolonged exposure to violence and disruption of education at critical stages of development has long-term impact on mental health, cognitive development, and the overall well-being of children, especially for children associated with armed forces and armed groups. Safe education in conflict and post-conflict settings must go beyond access to schooling. Quality, inclusive education can play a transformative role in healing trauma, strengthening social bonds, restoring a sense of normalcy, and breaking further cycles of violence, stigma, and marginalization. In this regard, practical action is required. This includes endorsing and implementing the Safe Schools Declaration, integrating education into humanitarian and peacebuilding responses, developing of comprehensive strategies to prevent and and respond to attacks on education, strengthening of the monitoring and reporting on attacks on education, ensuring long-term gender and age-sensitive and disability-inclusive support and protection to victims and survivors of attacks on education, facilitating the reintegration of children who have been forced out of school, addressing the disproportionate impact of education disruption on girls, securing adequate funding to create welcoming, safe, and inclusive learning spaces. We wish to highlight also the role of the Country Task Forces on Monitoring and Reporting, which lead the formal monitoring and reporting mechanism in the collection of timely, accurate, objective, and reliable information on attacks against educational facilities. can foster protection even in a complex global landscape because education is prevention, education is protection, education is ultimately peace. I thank you.

Chair.

Excellencies, distinguished briefers, Liberia thanks the Permanent Mission of Panama and co-sponsors for convening this important Area Formula meeting in observance of Rare Hand Day, keeping the plight of children affected by armed conflict at the forefront of our shared priorities. For Liberia, the implications are neither hypothetical nor remote. They are part of our national memory. We have witnessed within our own borders the devastating consequences of the recruitment and use of children in armed conflict. We have seen classrooms and schools destroyed and reduced to rubble. It is prevention. It is resilience. It is peacebuilding in its most practical form. Our conscience should be troubled by the alarming data before us of over 41,000 verified grave violations against children and a sharp rise in attacks on schools. When schools are attacked, occupied, or rendered inaccessible, children are pushed from structured environments into uncertainty and vulnerability. That vacuum is often filled by armed actors. The normative framework is clear: the Optional Protocol to the Convention on the Rights of the Child, the Geneva Conventions, and Security Council Resolution 1998 affirmed that schools are civilian objects and must be protected. In Liberia's own post-conflict recovery, we learned that the reintegration programs must be gender-sensitive, trauma-informed, and community-led. Girls who are survivors or victims of armed conflict face stigma. They require confidential, survivor-centered support and pathways back to education that respect dignity and prevent re-victimization. We must pursue accountability for all those who victimize— who commit violations against children during armed conflict. Liberia remains committed to advancing the children in armed conflict agenda and supports coherence between protection mandates and educational recovery efforts. We ask all parties to armed conflict to fully comply with the applicable international law, to respect and protect the civilian character of schools, and to take concrete and timely steps to ensure the continued provision of education for children in line with Security Council Resolution 2601. Ultimately, preventing the recruitment and use of children is not only a matter of compliance, it is a matter of political will. If we are serious about breaking the cycles of conflict, we must treat education not as an afterthought, to peace, but as its foundation. Let us ensure that every child in every town, village, and city, and even in the most fragile settings, can hold a book instead of a weapon, can be enlisted for an educational activity, not worried about being taken in captivity, can sit at a desk instead of standing at a checkpoint can imagine a future defined not by fear but by possibilities. Liberia stands ready to work with all partners to make safe education a reality for every child in conflict-affected settings, and I thank you.
I thank the delegation of Liberia for that statement, and I now give the floor to the delegation of Denmark.

Thank you, Chair.

Let me also thank the briefers and commend Panama and co-sponsors Greece, Liberia, Austria, Japan, and Uruguay for organizing today's meeting. Chair, every person who has benefited from an education knows its transformative power. This is true in Denmark, in Panama, here in New York, and across the world. But as we have heard today, it is especially true in conflict and post-conflict situations. The evidence is clear. The lived experience of children is clear. Education saves lives. It gives hope. It transforms nations. And it must be protected from attack. The international legal framework is clear on this. Yet attacks against schools are increasing whilst education and protection services are underfinanced. Against this backdrop, the international community, including the Security Council, must shoulder its responsibility. We should support the mandates and ensure the funding necessary to enable critical programming. We must collectively ensure that parties to conflict uphold international law, including international humanitarian law and international human rights law. Parties to conflict must commit to specific, structured steps to end and prevent grave violations against children and uphold accountability. Chair, we know that improvements in programming and increased evidence and data can help to reach these goals. For our part, Denmark will continue to stand up for international law. We will work to uphold existing normative and legal standards designed to protect children and ensure their right to education. We will work to equip the UN and partners with the necessary instruments to provide universal child protection and education. In closing, Chair, as we mark the Red Hand Day, let us not only reflect but recommit. We commit to the children in Haiti, who should be able to enjoy a safe learning environment without fear of being recruited by gangs; to the children in Sudan, who are attacked, starved, and displaced; and to the children in Ukraine, who must be free from indoctrination and militarization by Russia in the context of Russia's full-scale invasion— an invasion that marks 4 long years to this date. Denmark stands ready to work with all partners to this end. I thank you.
I thank the representative of Denmark for that statement, and I now give the floor to the representative of the United Kingdom.

Chair, the United Kingdom thanks Panama and the co-sponsors for convening this important meeting, and we thank our distinguished briefers for their remarks. Education is not only a fundamental right, it is one of the most effective tools we have to safeguard children in conflict and prevent grave violations. Yet in the past year, attacks on schools rose sharply, putting millions of children at risk and robbing them of the futures they deserve. We must do more to ensure that education remains safe, accessible, and uninterrupted. I will make 3 points. First, we call on all parties to conflict to adhere to international humanitarian law and end deliberate or indiscriminate attacks on schools. We urge full implementation of the Safe Schools Declaration and of the Political Declaration on Strengthening the Protection of Civilians from the Humanitarian Consequences Arising from the Use of Explosive Weapons in Populated Areas. Second, we must recognize that access to learning is indeed a shield. Without it, children are far more susceptible to recruitment, exploitation, sexual violence. The impacts on girls are particularly stark. We know that girls who cannot access education are at higher risk of sexual and gender-based violence, more likely to marry young, and less likely to be able to lead healthy, productive adult lives. Yet the scale of educational disruption due to conflict is staggering. In Sudan, around 90 million children are out of school. In Gaza, as we have heard, over 90% of education facilities have been damaged or destroyed. And in Ukraine today, on the 4th anniversary of Russia's full-scale invasion, too many children are unable to learn because their classrooms are dark and freezing. Working together to ensure educational access is critical to protecting children and building stability in these and other conflict settings. Third, the United Kingdom is proud to support global efforts to protect education in crisis settings, including through our work with Education Cannot Wait, which reached 8.8 million children with education and psychosocial support between 2023 and 2024, and through the Global Partnership for Education, supporting learning in Sudan, Palestine, Ukraine, and beyond. And in closing, Chair, we urge other member states to join us in supporting these vital efforts. I thank you.
I thank the representative of the United Kingdom for that statement, and I'm pleased now to give the floor to the representative of Colombia.

Thank you, Chair. Allow me to begin by expressing my thanks to Panama and the co-sponsors and the briefers. For Colombia, a country that has suffered the ravages of war in manifold forms and with firsthand experience of this issue, it is a duty to resolutely support all initiatives to address the scourge of child recruitment, all the more so as we are currently a Security Council member. Recruitment represents a grave violation of the rights of the child. It perpetuates cycles of violence, it weakens the social fabric, and it compromises prospects for a lasting peace. In this context, we recognize the central role of education, not only as a fundamental right but also as a tool for protection and prevention. Access to safe, inclusive, and quality education makes children less vulnerable to recruitment, and it provides real alternatives for development, dignity, and for their future. Schools should be safe spaces, never stages for violence or military objectives.
